newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Jospin leaves French defence firms wondering.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Jospin leaves French defence firms wondering.

text.p: Aerospace executives are hoping for clarification of the new French government's plans for the defence sector when Prime Minister Lionel Jospin addresses the Paris air show on Saturday.
The industry was left none the wiser on the Socialist-led government's policy on privatisation and defence consolidation after Jospin's keynote address on Thursday.
He said he did not favour state selloffs, unless national interests demanded it, but did not want to stop French state firms from striking partnerships with other European companies.

Industry executives are waiting to see what the new government will do with defence electronics firm Thomson-CSF, which was in the process of being sold by the previous government, and the planned merger of Aerospatiale with combat plane maker Dassault Aviation.
Few expect Jospin to give details on these crucial issues to the French and European industry.
"There are only questions and guesses on Aerospatiale and Dassault," a French aerospace executive said.
A merger of Dassault and Aerospatiale, followed by a privatisation of the new group, was a key plank in the French defence industry consolidation planned by the previous conservative government.
European firms agree they need to respond quickly to compete with the U.S. mega-mergers creating giants such as Boeing -McDonnell Douglas and Raytheon -Hughes.
But sovereignty issues and fear of job losses are slowing European attempts to forge corporate alliances. The debate over private versus public ownership is also hampering progress.

"The system is blocked because of the different status of Aerospatiale and Dassault," the executive said. A merger between public and private companies would require that one or the other change its status.
The government seems to be opposed to privatisations but cannot afford to nationalise Dassault.
Jospin also spoke on Thursday of a broad defence consolidation with an emphasis on European cooperation.

A second French aerospace executive took that as a positive sign, suggesting there will be an emphasis on more European collaboration at the programme level, along the lines of "50/50 shares or 30/30/30" with foreign partners.

In the absence of privatisations, those types of joint ventures may be encouraged or the government could put Thomson-CSF together with Aerospatiale in a vertical integration of Thomson's electronics skills with Aerospatiale's missiles.

But in time, pressure from private British and German companies like Dasa and British Aerospace Plc will be so great the French government will have to agree to at least partial privatisation, a French defence official said.
Even then, it is not clear if European partners would accept the French government retaining control, he said.

An analyst said he did not think any major private European players would take a stake in a state-controlled Aerospatiale. "I don't think any of the big companies would want to be a minority partner of the French state," he said.
Germany's defence minister, Volker Ruhe, said "if we want to create strong companies in the face of American competition in Europe, they need to be private companies."
